summary: Describes SASL, a method for adding authentication to connection-based protocols. A protocol includes a command to choose an authentication mechanism, and may optionally set up a security layer. It was replaced by RFC 4422 and RFC 4752.

plainLanguage.summary: SASL is a framework that lets a protocol built on a connection ask the other end to prove who they are, and then to encrypt the rest of the conversation. The protocol adds one command, and a named mechanism decides how the question and the answer look.

questions: what is a sasl security layer
subtitle: A way for a connection-based protocol to ask who is on the other end, and to encrypt what follows.

tldr.problem: Every connection-based protocol that wanted to know who its user was, and to protect the rest of the conversation, had to invent its own way of doing it.
tldr.mechanism: SASL defines a command that a protocol adds to identify and authenticate a user, a set of named mechanisms that define the challenge and response exchange, and a framing for a negotiated security layer that protects everything sent after the exchange.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines four mechanisms, rules for what a protocol must specify, and registration procedures for new ones. The RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 4422 and RFC 4752, and it was later updated by RFC 2444.

today: RFC 2222 is an October 1997 standards-track specification of SASL, and the RFC Editor index lists it as obsoleted by RFC 4422 and RFC 4752. It was later updated by RFC 2444.

sections.title: What SASL Does
sections.content:
The Simple Authentication and Security Layer is a method for adding authentication support to connection-based protocols. To use it, a protocol includes a command for identifying and authenticating a user to a server and for optionally negotiating protection of subsequent protocol interactions. If the use of a security layer is negotiated, that layer is inserted between the protocol and the connection.

The command has a required argument identifying a SASL mechanism. Mechanism names are strings of 1 to 20 characters, consisting of upper-case letters, digits, hyphens and underscores, and they must be registered with IANA. If the server supports the requested mechanism, it starts an authentication exchange, which consists of a series of server challenges and client responses specific to that mechanism. The challenges and responses are defined by the mechanisms as binary tokens of arbitrary length, and the protocol's profile then specifies how those tokens are encoded for transfer over the connection.

After receiving the authentication command or any client response, the server may issue a challenge, indicate failure, or indicate completion, and the profile says how the server shows which of the three it is doing. After a challenge, the client may issue a response or abort the exchange, and again the profile says how the client shows which.

During the exchange the mechanism performs the authentication, transmits an authorization identity, frequently known as a userid, from the client to the server, and negotiates the use of a mechanism-specific security layer. If a security layer is agreed, the mechanism must also define or negotiate the maximum cipher-text buffer size that each side is able to receive.

The transmitted authorization identity may be different from the identity in the client's authentication credentials. That permits agents such as proxy servers to authenticate with their own credentials while requesting the access privileges of the identity they are proxying for, and transmitting an empty authorization identity tells the server to derive one from the client's credentials.

If a security layer is negotiated, it applies to all subsequent data sent over the connection, taking effect immediately after the last response of the authentication exchange for data sent by the client, and after the completion indication for data sent by the server. The protocol stream is then processed by the security layer into buffers of cipher-text, and each buffer is transferred as a stream of octets prepended with a four octet field in network byte order giving the length of the buffer that follows. The length of a cipher-text buffer must be no larger than the maximum size defined or negotiated by the other side.
sections.plainLanguage: The client names a mechanism, the server sends challenges, the client answers, and the server says whether it is satisfied. If the mechanism includes protection, everything after that point is wrapped in it, with a length prefix on each block.

sections.title: What a Protocol Must Specify
sections.content:
To use this specification, a protocol definition must supply five things.

First, a service name, selected from the IANA registry of service elements for the GSSAPI host-based service name form. Second, a definition of the command that initiates the authentication exchange, which must have as a parameter the mechanism name being selected by the client. The command should have an optional parameter giving an initial response, which lets the client avoid a round trip when using a mechanism defined to have the client send data first; when that parameter is sent and the selected mechanism is defined to have the server start with an initial challenge, the command fails.

Third, a definition of the method by which the authentication exchange is carried out, including how the challenges and responses are encoded, how the server indicates completion or failure, how the client aborts an exchange, and how the exchange method interacts with any line length limits in the protocol. Fourth, identification of the octet where any negotiated security layer starts to take effect, in both directions. Fifth, a specification of how the authorization identity passed from the client to the server is to be interpreted.
sections.plainLanguage: SASL leaves the details to the protocol that uses it. A protocol has to say which command starts the exchange, how the pieces are carried, where the protection begins, and what the userid means.

sections.title: Three Special Cases
sections.content:
Some mechanisms specify that the first data sent in the exchange comes from the client. If a profile permits the initiating command to carry an initial client response, that parameter should be used with such mechanisms. If the parameter is not given, or the profile does not permit it, the server issues a challenge with no data, and the client's response to that challenge is used as the initial client response, after which the server proceeds to send the next challenge, indicate completion, or indicate failure.

Some mechanisms specify that server challenge data be sent to the client along with an indication of successful completion, for example data that authenticates the server to the client. If the profile does not permit the server challenge to be returned with a success indication, the server issues the challenge without it, the client responds with no data, and the server then indicates successful completion after receiving that empty response.

Unless the profile says otherwise, only one successful SASL negotiation may occur in a protocol session, so once an authentication exchange has completed successfully, further attempts to start one fail. In the case where a profile explicitly permits multiple successful negotiations, there may never be multiple security layers in effect at the same time: if a security layer is in effect and a subsequent negotiation selects no security layer, the original layer remains in effect, and if a subsequent negotiation selects a second security layer, that one replaces the first.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mechanisms want the client to speak first, and some want to send a last word that proves who the server is. The rules above let a protocol that cannot carry those shapes work with them anyway, and they stop a session negotiating protection twice.

sections.title: The Mechanisms
sections.content:
Four mechanisms are defined in this document.

The Kerberos version 4 mechanism is named KERBEROS_V4. The first challenge is a random 32-bit number in network byte order, and the client responds with a Kerberos ticket and an authenticator for the principal service.hostname@realm, where the service is the name from the protocol's profile and the hostname is the first component of the server's host name in lower case. The server verifies the ticket and the challenge, then returns 8 octets of data encrypted with DES in ECB mode under the session key: the incremented checksum, a bit-mask of the security layers it supports, and the maximum cipher-text buffer size it can receive. The client then sends back the original checksum, the security layer it has selected, its own maximum buffer size and the authorization identity, padded to a multiple of eight octets and encrypted with DES in PCBC mode.

The GSSAPI mechanism, named GSSAPI, covers all mechanisms employing the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface, and the RFC describes both the client side and the server side of that exchange and its security layer. The S/Key mechanism is named SKEY and provides no security layers at all, using a one-time password. The External mechanism, named EXTERNAL, has the client send an initial response carrying the authorization identity, and the server uses information from outside SASL, such as IPsec or TLS, to decide whether the client is allowed to authenticate as that identity. If the client sends the empty string as the authorization identity, the identity is to be derived from the credentials in the system providing the external authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Four ways of doing it are defined: Kerberos version 4, the standard security interface, one-time passwords, and a mode that trusts something else on the connection, such as TLS, to have already identified the client.

sections.title: Registering a Mechanism
sections.content:
Registration of a mechanism is done by filling in the template and sending it in. IANA has the right to reject obviously bogus registrations but performs no review of the claims made in the registration form. There is no naming convention for SASL mechanisms, so any name that fits the syntax can be registered, although the registration procedures do not require it, authors of mechanisms are encouraged to seek community review and comment whenever that is feasible, and mechanisms intended for widespread use should be standardized through the normal IETF process when appropriate.

Comments on a registered mechanism should first be sent to the owner of the mechanism, and a submitter who has made a reasonable attempt to contact the owner may ask IANA to attach the comment to the registration itself.

Once a registration has been published, the author may request a change to its definition, following the same procedure as the registration request. The owner of a mechanism may pass responsibility to another person or agency by informing IANA, and that can be done without discussion or review. The IESG may reassign responsibility for a mechanism, most commonly so that changes can be made when the author of the registration has died, moved out of contact, or is otherwise unable to make changes that are important to the community. Registrations may not be deleted: a mechanism that is no longer believed appropriate for use is declared OBSOLETE by a change to its intended use field, and is clearly marked in the lists published by IANA. The IESG is considered to be the owner of all mechanisms that are on the IETF standards track.
sections.plainLanguage: A mechanism name is claimed at IANA, and it stays claimed. If a mechanism turns out to be a bad idea, it is marked obsolete rather than removed, and the IESG takes over anything that is on the standards track.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security issues are discussed throughout the memo. The mechanisms that support integrity protection are designed so that the negotiation of the security layer and the authorization identity is integrity protected, which protects against an active attacker hijacking the connection and modifying the authentication exchange to negotiate a plaintext connection.

When a server or client supports several mechanisms of different security strength, an active attacker can cause a party to use the least secure one supported. To protect against this, a client or server that supports mechanisms of different strengths should have a configurable minimum strength that it will use. It is not sufficient for this check to be on the server alone, because an active attacker can change which mechanisms the client sees as being supported, causing the client to send credentials for its weakest supported mechanism.

The client's selection of a mechanism is done in the clear and may be modified by an active attacker, so new mechanisms should be designed such that an active attacker cannot obtain an authentication with weaker security properties by modifying the mechanism name or the challenges and responses. Any protocol interactions before authentication are performed in the clear and may be modified by an active attacker, so where a client selects integrity protection it is important that any security-sensitive protocol negotiations be performed after authentication is complete, and protocols should be designed so that negotiations performed before authentication are either ignored or revalidated once authentication is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The weak point is the start of the conversation, which is not protected. Someone on the path can try to talk the client into using the weakest method it supports, so both ends should insist on a minimum strength, and anything sensitive should be negotiated only after the authentication is done.
